Al-Bukhari narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ sent a man in command of a detachment (sariyyah). He used to lead his companions in prayer and would finish his recitation with ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. When they returned, they mentioned this to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Ask him why he does that." They asked him, and he said: "Because it is the attribute of the Most Gracious, and I love to recite it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Tell him that Allah, the Exalted, loves him."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Say: He is Allah, the One is equal to a third of the Qur'an." It was also narrated by al-Bukhari in a different context.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that "the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'O Muhammad, tell us the lineage of your Lord.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this surah."

(p-6295) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[1–4] ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]

﴿Say: He﴾ means: the true report, confirmed by proof, about which there is no doubt. This is what the grammarians call the "story" (qissah), or the "matter" (hadith), or the "affair" (sha'n). Abu al-Su'ud said: The reason for placing it in this position, although no antecedent has been mentioned, is to indicate that it is so well known and prominent that everyone recalls it, every pointer points to it, and every pronoun refers back to it. ﴿Allah is One﴾, that is, one in divinity (uluhiyyah) and lordship (rububiyyah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ahad" (One) means "wahid" (one). Ibn al-Athir said: "al-Ahad" among His names, exalted is He, is the Unique who has always been alone, with no other with Him. Its hamza is a substitute for a waw, and its original form is "wahad," because it derives from wahdah (oneness).

In al-Misbah it is said: "ahad" is synonymous with "wahid" in two positions, by transmitted usage. The first: describing the Name of the Creator, exalted is He. One says: He is al-Wahid and He is al-Ahad, because He is exclusively characterized by oneness (ahadiyyah), so no other shares it with Him. For this reason, no one other than Allah, exalted is He, is described by it; one does not say "a man ahad" or "a dirham ahad" or the like.

The second position: the numerals, by prevalence and frequent usage; one says "ahad wa-'ishrun" and "wahid wa-'ishrun." In other contexts the difference between them in usage is that "ahad" is used to negate what is mentioned with it, so it is used only in negation, because it contains generality, as in: "No one (ahad) stood." Or when it is annexed, as in: "None (ahad) of the three stood." "Wahid" is the name for the first of a series of numbers, and it is used in affirmation, both annexed and unannexed; one says: "A certain (wahid) man of the people came to me." End of quotation.

(p-6296) Al-Azhari said: "Wahid" is among the attributes of Allah, exalted is He; its meaning is that He has no second. It is permissible to describe a thing as "wahid." But "ahad" is not used to describe anything other than Allah, exalted is He, because this noble name belongs exclusively to Him, may His praise be exalted.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: The predicate is indefinite (nukkira) because the intention is to inform about Allah that He is one, not that there is no one else besides Him. Oneness belongs to each individual; you say: "There is no one (ahad) in the house," meaning that no one among the people is in it. What the addressees were claiming was plurality within His essence, so He wished to negate that by saying He is "one." This is an affirmation contrary to what the two principles (usul) believers hold, such as the Magians, and what those who hold to the Trinity believe, both among themselves and others. Ibn Taymiyyah will later present another discussion on the secret of choosing indefiniteness.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] means: He to whom one turns in needs and to whom one directs desires, because the ultimate of lordship ends with Him. Al-Ghazali said this in al-Maqsad al-Asna. Likewise Ibn Jarir said: "al-Samad" among the Arabs is the lord (sayyid) to whom one turns, who has no one above him, and likewise their nobles are called by it. From this is the poet's verse:

"Has not the mourner come at dawn with news of the two best of Bani Asad,
of 'Amr ibn Mas'ud and of the eminent lord al-Samad?"

Al-Shihab said: It is "fa'al" in the sense of "maf'ul," and "samada" means "qasada" (to intend), so it is transitive by itself, and with the lam and with ila.

Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Regarding al-Samad, the early generations (al-salaf) held several opinions, which may seem to be different, but they are not; rather all of them are correct. The most well known of them are two:

The first: that al-Samad is the one who has no hollow (jawf).
The second: that He is the lord to whom one turns in needs.

The first is the view of most of the early generations among the Companions and the Successors, and of a group of the linguists. The second is the view of a group of the early and later scholars and of the majority of the lexicographers.

(p-6297) Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, expanded on the source of this term, its derivation, and what is transmitted about it, until he said:

The lam was added to "al-Samad" but not to "ahad," because among existing things there is nothing called "ahad" in affirmation, singular and unannexed; no entity is described by it except Allah alone. It is used for other than Allah only in negation, in annexation, and in the unrestricted numeral. As for the name "al-Samad," the linguists used it of created beings, as mentioned earlier. So He did not say "samad" but said ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2], clarifying that He alone is entitled to be the Samad, not what is other than Him, for He is the one who deserves His ultimate perfection. A created being, though it may be samad in some respects, does not truly possess the reality of samadiyyah, because it accepts division and fragmentation, and it is also in need of other than itself, for everything other than Allah is in need of Him in every respect. No one is someone to whom everything turns while he turns to nothing except Allah. In created things there is only what can be divided, separated, split, and detached, part from part. But Allah, glory be to Him, is the Samad to whom none of that can apply; rather the reality and perfection of samadiyyah belong to Him alone, necessarily and inseparably. It is impossible for His samadiyyah to be absent in any way, just as it is impossible for His oneness to be doubled in any way. End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The repetition of the Glorious Name is to indicate that whoever does not possess these attributes is far from deserving divinity. The sentence is left without a conjunction because it is like a conclusion (natijah) of the first. First He stated His divinity (uluhiyyah), which entails all the attributes of perfection; then His oneness (ahadiyyah), which requires His transcendence above any trace of plurality and composition in any respect, and above any supposition of sharing in the essence and its properties; then His samadiyyah, which requires His essential self-sufficiency (istighna') from all other than Him and the need of all creatures for Him in their existence, their continuance, and all their conditions. This is to establish the truth and to guide them to His clear path. Then He explicitly mentioned some of what falls under what was previously stated, with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿He begets not﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3], refuting the claims of the slanderers concerning the angels and the Messiah. For this reason the negation came in the past tense form, meaning: no child has issued from Him, because nothing is of His kind, so that He could have a consort of His kind and they would beget. As His words, exalted is He, affirm: ﴿How can He have a child when He has no consort?﴾ And He has no need of anything that would help Him or succeed Him, because need and perishing are impossible for Him, glory be to Him. End of quotation.

(p-6298) Ibn Taymiyyah said: What He, glory be to Him, informed about includes His transcendence and sanctification above what they attributed to Him of begetting, in all its forms, whether they called it physical or intellectual. Like the Sabian philosophers claim about the generation of the ten intellects and the nine celestial souls, concerning which they are in dispute: are they substances or accidents? They sometimes make the intellects equivalent to males and the souls equivalent to females, and they make these their fathers, their mothers, their gods, and their nearest lords. This resembles the saying of the polytheists of the Arabs and others, who attributed to Him sons and daughters. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah, though He created them, and they falsely attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glorified is He and high above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100]. He also said: ﴿Surely they say out of their own lies﴾ [al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-Saffat: 152]. They used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Likewise these people claim that the souls are the angels, and that they are generated from Allah. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they attribute daughters to Allah—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57]. The verses on this are many.

His words ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] are a negation of any relation (nasab) encompassing Him from every direction. He is the First, to whom no parent preceded, and the Last, after whom no child will come to be from Him. The Imam (al-Razi) said: His words ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ clearly refute what some followers of religions claim: that a son of Allah could be a god, worshipped with the worship due to God, and that the Divine is intended in him. Rather, the extremists among them are not ashamed to call his mother "the Mother of the Powerful God." For the begotten is created and comes into being only through a temperament (mizaj), and he is not safe from the consequence of extinction. The claim that he is eternal together with his father is something that cannot be conceived. He, glory be to Him, is far above that.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4] means: no one equal to Him exists who could match Him, whether a consort or otherwise. The Imam said: "Kufu'" means one who is equal to and similar to Him in action and power. This is a negation of what some idolaters believe about, for example, Satan. In this surah He has negated all kinds of association (shirk) and established all the foundations of tawhid and tanzih. Ibn Jarir said: "al-kufu'," "al-kafi'," and "al-kifa'" are one and the same in the speech of the Arabs; they mean equal and like.

It is also read "kufuwan" with a damma on the kaf and the fa', and the hamza changed into a waw. It is also read with the fa' sukun and with the hamza; these are two well-known readings and two famous dialects. The word "lahu" is a complement to "kufuwan," placed before it although its natural place is after it, for emphasis, because the intention is to negate equal recompense from His essence, exalted is He. As for the delay of the subject of "kana," it is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawasil).

Benefits from this surah:

The first: Al-Shihab said: If you ask: the one addressed by "Say" (qul), when he complies, should only utter what is said. Why is "Say" among what is recited in it and in similar passages? I answer: The one commanded, whether specified or not, is commanded to affirm what is said, so He affirmed the saying in order to indicate the obligation of what is said and the necessity of affirming it throughout the ages.

The second: Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said: Some proponents of innovated speculative theology (kalam) have argued from His words ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] that the Lord, exalted is He, is a body (jism). Like some who agreed with Hisham ibn al-Hakam, Muhammad ibn Karram, and others, they said: He is samad, and the samad is that which has no hollow. This applies only to solid bodies, which have no hollow, such as mountains, rocks, and what is made of columns of stone. For this reason it was said in its explanation that He is that from which nothing comes out and into which nothing enters, and who neither eats nor drinks. The negation of this is conceivable only of what is a body.

They also said: The root of "samad" is gathering, and from it comes "tasmid al-mal" (piling up of wealth). This is conceivable only of a gathered body. But the negators said: "al-Samad" is the one to whom division and separation cannot apply, and every body in the world is subject to division and separation. They also said: "al-Ahad" is the one who does not accept partition or division, and every body in the world is subject to separation, partition, and division. They said: If you say He is a body, He would be composed (murakkab) and assembled (mu'allaf) (p-6300) of single particles (jawahir fardah) or of matter and form. Whatever is composed and assembled of other things is in need of them, and He, glory be to Him, is the samad, and the samad is the one free of need of others. So the composite cannot be samad. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: Some of the ignorant Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) have used this verse as evidence that God, exalted is He, is a body. This is false, because we have already shown that His being One (aḥad) contradicts His being a body. The introduction to this verse indicates that the meaning of al-Samad cannot be this meaning. Moreover, al-Samad with this interpretation is a attribute of compact bodies, and God is exalted above that. Therefore it must be taken in its metaphorical sense. That is because a body of this kind is unaffected and untouched by others, and this points to His being, glorified is He, necessarily existent in His essence, unchangeable in His existence, His permanence, and all His attributes. End of quote.

I say: the correct interpretation of al-Samad is what we mentioned first, which is what Ibn Jarir and others related from the Arabs regarding its meaning. Once this is established, one should not rely on this second interpretation or its implications.

Third: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Just as it is obligatory to declare the Lord free of every deficiency and defect, it is obligatory to declare Him free of having any of the creatures resemble Him in any of the attributes of perfection that are affirmed for Him. These two types together comprise the declaration of God's transcendence that is obligatory. This surah indicates both types. His saying "One" (aḥad), from His saying ﴿And there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4], negates likeness and sharing. His saying "al-Samad" encompasses all attributes of perfection, and deficiencies in general are negated of God, exalted is He. Everything that is specific to the created being is among the deficiencies from which the Lord must be declared free. This is unlike what is ascribed to the Lord, and the servant is described with what befits him, such as knowledge, power, mercy and the like, for these are not deficiencies. Rather, whatever of these meanings is established for God, it is established for Him in a manner that none of the creatures comes close to, let alone resembles Him in it. Indeed, what God created in Paradise of foods, drinks and garments does not resemble what He created in this world, even though they agree in name, since both are created. Thus the Creator, exalted is He, is further removed from resembling the creatures than one created thing is from another created thing. God has named Himself Knowing (ʿAlim), Forbearing (Halim), Kind (Ra'uf), Merciful (Rahim), Hearing (Sami'), Seeing (Basir), Mighty (ʿAziz), King (Malik), Compeller (Jabbar), and Proud (Mutakabbir), and He has also named some of His creatures with these names, while knowing that the one named with these names among the creatures is in no way resembling the Creator, majestic is His majesty, in anything.

(p-6301) Fourth: We have already mentioned what has been transmitted in the hadith that ""Surat al-Ikhlas equals one third of the Qur'an"". 

Scholars have mentioned several reasons for this, among them what Abu al-ʿAbbas ibn Surayj said: the Qur'an was revealed in three categories: one third concerns rulings (ahkam), one third is promise and warning, and one third is names and attributes. This surah comprises the names and attributes. Al-Ghazali said in (Jawahir al-Qur'an): The major concerns of the Qur'an are the knowledge of God, the knowledge of the Hereafter, and the knowledge of the Straight Path. These three knowledges are the major ones, and the rest are subsidiary. Surat al-Ikhlas includes one of the three, namely the knowledge of God, and His sanctification and His oneness, free from any partner in genus and species. This is the meaning of the negation of origin, offspring and equal. 

He said: The description "al-Samad" suggests that He is the Master to whom no one is turned in existence for needs other than Him. Yes, it does not contain mention of the Hereafter and the Straight Path, so it equals one third of the Qur'an, i.e., one third of the principles of the Qur'an, as he said: ""Hajj is ʿArafah"", meaning it is the principal and the rest are subordinate.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Zad al-Maʿad): ""The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Dawn Sunnah and the Witr the two surahs al-Ikhlas and al-Kafirun"", and these two are the ones that comprise the oneness of knowledge and action, the oneness of knowledge and will, and the oneness of belief and intention. Surat al-Ikhlas includes the oneness of belief and knowledge, what must be affirmed for the Lord, exalted is He, of oneness (ahadiyyah) which negates any sharing in any way whatsoever, and of self-sufficiency (samadiyyah) which affirms for Him all attributes of perfection that no deficiency reaches in any way, and the negation of offspring and parent, which is a necessary consequence of self-sufficiency, His independence and His oneness, and the negation of equal (kufu'), which entails the negation of a similar, an equal and a peer. Thus this surah includes the affirmation of every perfection for Him, the negation of every deficiency from Him, the negation of affirming a like or an equal to Him in His perfection, and the negation of any partner whatsoever. These principles are the comprehensive elements of the scholarly, doctrinal oneness that sets its adherent apart from all sects of misguidance and polytheism. For this reason it equals one third of the Qur'an, since the Qur'an revolves around information (khabar) and injunction (insha'), and injunction is of three kinds: command, prohibition, and permission. Information is of two kinds: information about the Creator, exalted is He, His names, attributes and rulings, and information about His creation. Surat al-Ikhlas purified the information about Him (p-6302) and about His names and attributes, so it equals one third of the Qur'an, and it purified the believing reciter from scholarly polytheism, just as Surat "Say: O disbelievers" purified from practical, volitional, intentional polytheism. Since knowledge precedes action, and is its leader, its guide, its driver, the one that governs it and places it in its ranks, Surat "Say: He is God, One" equals one third of the Qur'an, and the hadiths on this nearly reach the level of being mutawatir. "Say: O disbelievers" [al-Kafirun: 1] equals one quarter of the Qur'an. In al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet: ""'When the earth is shaken' equals half the Qur'an, 'Say: He is God, One' equals one third of the Qur'an, and 'Say: O disbelievers' equals one quarter of the Qur'an."" Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak and said: its chain is sound.

Since practical, volitional polytheism is more dominant over souls because of their following of their desires, and many of them commit it knowing its harm and falsehood, due to the worldly aims they gain from it, its removal and uprooting from them is harder and more difficult than uprooting and removing scholarly polytheism, because the latter disappears through knowledge and proof, and its adherent cannot know a thing other than as it is, unlike the polytheism of will and intention, for its adherent commits what knowledge shows to be false and harmful, due to the dominance of his desire and the domination of the authority of lust and anger over his self. Hence the emphasis and repetition in the surah "Say: O disbelievers", which includes the removal of practical polytheism, is equivalent to what comes in the surah "Say: He is God, One".

Since the Qur'an is two halves: one half concerning this world, its rulings, what relates to them, and events occurring in it, including the actions of the responsible and others, and one half concerning the Hereafter and what takes place in it; and since Surat "When the earth is shaken" is purified from beginning to end for this second half, mentioning only the Hereafter and what occurs regarding the conditions of the earth and its inhabitants, it equals half the Qur'an. Hence this hadith is most fitting to be sound. And God knows best.

(p-6303) Fifth: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Most scholars hold that Surat "Say: He is God, One" is Meccan, and it has been mentioned in the occasions of its revelation that the polytheists in Mecca asked about it, and that disbelievers among the People of the Book, the Jews, asked in Medina. There is no contradiction, for God revealed it in Mecca first, then when asked something similar He revealed it again. This is among what a group of scholars have mentioned, and they said: a verse or surah may be revealed twice or more. What is mentioned among the various occasions of revelation may all be true, and what is meant by this is that when a cause suitable to it arose, Gabriel descended and recited it to him to inform him that it contains the answer to that cause, even though the Messenger already knew it beforehand. End of quote.

The investigation into the meaning of revelation, in a way that removes such apparent contradictions, has already been detailed in the introduction to this tafsir and in other places within it, so refer back to it.

For this noble surah there are separate tafsirs, and among the best are two books by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah: one on its tafsir, and the second on the secret of its equalling one third of the Qur'an, so keep both. And God is the Guide.

But Allah, glory be to Him, is the Samad to whom none of that can apply; rather the reality and perfection of samadiyyah belong to Him alone, necessarily and inseparably. It is impossible for His samadiyyah to be absent in any way, just as it is impossible for His oneness to be doubled in any way. End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The repetition of the Glorious Name is to indicate that whoever does not possess these attributes is far from deserving divinity. The sentence is left without a conjunction because it is like a conclusion (natijah) of the first. First He stated His divinity (uluhiyyah), which entails all the attributes of perfection; then His oneness (ahadiyyah), which requires His transcendence above any trace of plurality and composition in any respect, and above any supposition of sharing in the essence and its properties; then His samadiyyah, which requires His essential self-sufficiency (istighna') from all other than Him and the need of all creatures for Him in their existence, their continuance, and all their conditions. End of quotation.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4] means: no one equal to Him exists who could match Him, whether a consort or otherwise. The Imam said: "Kufu'" means one who is equal to and similar to Him in action and power. This is a negation of what some idolaters believe about, for example, Satan. Benefits from this surah:

The first: Al-Shihab said: If you ask: the one addressed by "Say" (qul), when he complies, should only utter what is said. Why is "Say" among what is recited in it and in similar passages? I answer: The one commanded, whether specified or not, is commanded to affirm what is said, so He affirmed the saying in order to indicate the obligation of what is said and the necessity of affirming it throughout the ages.

The second: Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said: Some proponents of innovated speculative theology (kalam) have argued from His words ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] that the Lord, exalted is He, is a body (jism). Like some who agreed with Hisham ibn al-Hakam, Muhammad ibn Karram, and others, they said: He is samad, and the samad is that which has no hollow. This applies only to solid bodies, which have no hollow, such as mountains, rocks, and what is made of columns of stone. For this reason it was said in its explanation that He is that from which nothing comes out and into which nothing enters, and who neither eats nor drinks. The negation of this is conceivable only of what is a body.

They also said: The root of "samad" is gathering, and from it comes "tasmid al-mal" (piling up of wealth). This is conceivable only of a gathered body. But the negators said: "al-Samad" is the one to whom division and separation cannot apply, and every body in the world is subject to division and separation. They also said: "al-Ahad" is the one who does not accept partition or division, and every body in the world is subject to separation, partition, and division. They said: If you say He is a body, He would be composed (murakkab) and assembled (mu'allaf) (p-6300) of single particles (jawahir fardah) or of matter and form. Whatever is composed and assembled of other things is in need of them, and He, glory be to Him, is the samad, and the samad is the one free of need of others. So the composite cannot be samad. End of quotation.

Al-Razi said: Some of the ignorant Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) have used this verse as evidence that God, exalted is He, is a body. This is false, because we have already shown that His being One (aḥad) contradicts His being a body. The introduction to this verse indicates that the meaning of al-Samad cannot be this meaning. Moreover, al-Samad with this interpretation is a attribute of compact bodies, and God is exalted above that. Therefore it must be taken in its metaphorical sense. That is because a body of this kind is unaffected and untouched by others, and this points to His being, glorified is He, necessarily existent in His essence, unchangeable in His existence, His permanence, and all His attributes. End of quote.

I say: the correct interpretation of al-Samad is what we mentioned first, which is what Ibn Jarir and others related from the Arabs regarding its meaning. Once this is established, one should not rely on this second interpretation or its implications.

Third: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Just as it is obligatory to declare the Lord free of every deficiency and defect, it is obligatory to declare Him free of having any of the creatures resemble Him in any of the attributes of perfection that are affirmed for Him. These two types together comprise the declaration of God's transcendence that is obligatory. This surah indicates both types. His saying "One" (aḥad), from His saying ﴿And there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4], negates likeness and sharing. His saying "al-Samad" encompasses all attributes of perfection, and deficiencies in general are negated of God, exalted is He. Everything that is specific to the created being is among the deficiencies from which the Lord must be declared free. This is unlike what is ascribed to the Lord, and the servant is described with what befits him, such as knowledge, power, mercy and the like, for these are not deficiencies. Rather, whatever of these meanings is established for God, it is established for Him in a manner that none of the creatures comes close to, let alone resembles Him in it. Indeed, what God created in Paradise of foods, drinks and garments does not resemble what He created in this world, even though they agree in name, since both are created. Thus the Creator, exalted is He, is further removed from resembling the creatures than one created thing is from another created thing. God has named Himself Knowing (ʿAlim), Forbearing (Halim), Kind (Ra'uf), Merciful (Rahim), Hearing (Sami'), Seeing (Basir), Mighty (ʿAziz), King (Malik), Compeller (Jabbar), and Proud (Mutakabbir), and He has also named some of His creatures with these names, while knowing that the one named with these names among the creatures is in no way resembling the Creator, majestic is His majesty, in anything.

This surah comprises the names and attributes. Al-Ghazali said in (Jawahir al-Qur'an): The major concerns of the Qur'an are the knowledge of God, the knowledge of the Hereafter, and the knowledge of the Straight Path. These three knowledges are the major ones, and the rest are subsidiary. Surat al-Ikhlas includes one of the three, namely the knowledge of God, and His sanctification and His oneness, free from any partner in genus and species. This is the meaning of the negation of origin, offspring and equal. 

He said: The description "al-Samad" suggests that He is the Master to whom no one is turned in existence for needs other than Him. Yes, it does not contain mention of the Hereafter and the Straight Path, so it equals one third of the Qur'an, i.e., one third of the principles of the Qur'an, as he said: ""Hajj is ʿArafah"", meaning it is the principal and the rest are subordinate.

Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak and said: its chain is sound.

Since practical, volitional polytheism is more dominant over souls because of their following of their desires, and many of them commit it knowing its harm and falsehood, due to the worldly aims they gain from it, its removal and uprooting from them is harder and more difficult than uprooting and removing scholarly polytheism, because the latter disappears through knowledge and proof, and its adherent cannot know a thing other than as it is, unlike the polytheism of will and intention, for its adherent commits what knowledge shows to be false and harmful, due to the dominance of his desire and the domination of the authority of lust and anger over his self. Hence the emphasis and repetition in the surah "Say: O disbelievers", which includes the removal of practical polytheism, is equivalent to what comes in the surah "Say: He is God, One".

Hence this hadith is most fitting to be sound. And God knows best.

(p-6303) Fifth: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Most scholars hold that Surat "Say: He is God, One" is Meccan, and it has been mentioned in the occasions of its revelation that the polytheists in Mecca asked about it, and that disbelievers among the People of the Book, the Jews, asked in Medina. There is no contradiction, for God revealed it in Mecca first, then when asked something similar He revealed it again. This is among what a group of scholars have mentioned, and they said: a verse or surah may be revealed twice or more. What is mentioned among the various occasions of revelation may all be true, and what is meant by this is that when a cause suitable to it arose, Gabriel descended and recited it to him to inform him that it contains the answer to that cause, even though the Messenger already knew it beforehand. In al-Misbah it is said: "ahad" is synonymous with "wahid" in two positions, by transmitted usage. The first: describing the Name of the Creator, exalted is He. One says: He is al-Wahid and He is al-Ahad, because He is exclusively characterized by oneness (ahadiyyah), so no other shares it with Him. Al-Razi said: Some of the ignorant Mushabbihah (anthropomorphists) have used this verse as evidence that God, exalted is He, is a body. This is false, because we have already shown that His being One (aḥad) contradicts His being a body. The introduction to this verse indicates that the meaning of al-Samad cannot be this meaning. Moreover, al-Samad with this interpretation is a attribute of compact bodies, and God is exalted above that. Therefore it must be taken in its metaphorical sense. That is because a body of this kind is unaffected and untouched by others, and this points to His being, glorified is He, necessarily existent in His essence, unchangeable in His existence, His permanence, and all His attributes. End of quote.

I say: the correct interpretation of al-Samad is what we mentioned first, which is what Ibn Jarir and others related from the Arabs regarding its meaning. Once this is established, one should not rely on this second interpretation or its implications.

Third: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Just as it is obligatory to declare the Lord free of every deficiency and defect, it is obligatory to declare Him free of having any of the creatures resemble Him in any of the attributes of perfection that are affirmed for Him. These two types together comprise the declaration of God's transcendence that is obligatory. This surah indicates both types. His saying "One" (aḥad), from His saying ﴿And there is none comparable to Him, anyone﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4], negates likeness and sharing. His saying "al-Samad" encompasses all attributes of perfection, and deficiencies in general are negated of God, exalted is He. Everything that is specific to the created being is among the deficiencies from which the Lord must be declared free. This is unlike what is ascribed to the Lord, and the servant is described with what befits him, such as knowledge, power, mercy and the like, for these are not deficiencies. Rather, whatever of these meanings is established for God, it is established for Him in a manner that none of the creatures comes close to, let alone resembles Him in it. Indeed, what God created in Paradise of foods, drinks and garments does not resemble what He created in this world, even though they agree in name, since both are created. Thus the Creator, exalted is He, is further removed from resembling the creatures than one created thing is from another created thing. God has named Himself Knowing (ʿAlim), Forbearing (Halim), Kind (Ra'uf), Merciful (Rahim), Hearing (Sami'), Seeing (Basir), Mighty (ʿAziz), King (Malik), Compeller (Jabbar), and Proud (Mutakabbir), and He has also named some of His creatures with these names, while knowing that the one named with these names among the creatures is in no way resembling the Creator, majestic is His majesty, in anything.

(p-6301) Fourth: We have already mentioned what has been transmitted in the hadith that ""Surat al-Ikhlas equals one third of the Qur'an"". 

Scholars have mentioned several reasons for this, among them what Abu al-ʿAbbas ibn Surayj said: the Qur'an was revealed in three categories: one third concerns rulings (ahkam), one third is promise and warning, and one third is names and attributes. This surah comprises the names and attributes. Al-Ghazali said in (Jawahir al-Qur'an): The major concerns of the Qur'an are the knowledge of God, the knowledge of the Hereafter, and the knowledge of the Straight Path. These three knowledges are the major ones, and the rest are subsidiary. Surat al-Ikhlas includes one of the three, namely the knowledge of God, and His sanctification and His oneness, free from any partner in genus and species. This is the meaning of the negation of origin, offspring and equal. 

He said: The description "al-Samad" suggests that He is the Master to whom no one is turned in existence for needs other than Him. Yes, it does not contain mention of the Hereafter and the Straight Path, so it equals one third of the Qur'an, i.e., one third of the principles of the Qur'an, as he said: ""Hajj is ʿArafah"", meaning it is the principal and the rest are subordinate.

Ibn al-Qayyim said in (Zad al-Maʿad): ""The Prophet ﷺ used to recite in the Dawn Sunnah and the Witr the two surahs al-Ikhlas and al-Kafirun"", and these two are the ones that comprise the oneness of knowledge and action, the oneness of knowledge and will, and the oneness of belief and intention. Surat al-Ikhlas includes the oneness of belief and knowledge, what must be affirmed for the Lord, exalted is He, of oneness (ahadiyyah) which negates any sharing in any way whatsoever, and of self-sufficiency (samadiyyah) which affirms for Him all attributes of perfection that no deficiency reaches in any way, and the negation of offspring and parent, which is a necessary consequence of self-sufficiency, His independence and His oneness, and the negation of equal (kufu'), which entails the negation of a similar, an equal and a peer. Thus this surah includes the affirmation of every perfection for Him, the negation of every deficiency from Him, the negation of affirming a like or an equal to Him in His perfection, and the negation of any partner whatsoever. These principles are the comprehensive elements of the scholarly, doctrinal oneness that sets its adherent apart from all sects of misguidance and polytheism. For this reason it equals one third of the Qur'an, since the Qur'an revolves around information (khabar) and injunction (insha'), and injunction is of three kinds: command, prohibition, and permission. Information is of two kinds: information about the Creator, exalted is He, His names, attributes and rulings, and information about His creation. Surat al-Ikhlas purified the information about Him (p-6302) and about His names and attributes, so it equals one third of the Qur'an, and it purified the believing reciter from scholarly polytheism, just as Surat "Say: O disbelievers" purified from practical, volitional, intentional polytheism. Since knowledge precedes action, and is its leader, its guide, its driver, the one that governs it and places it in its ranks, Surat "Say: He is God, One" equals one third of the Qur'an, and the hadiths on this nearly reach the level of being mutawatir. "Say: O disbelievers" [al-Kafirun: 1] equals one quarter of the Qur'an. In al-Tirmidhi, from the narration of Ibn ʿAbbas, may God be pleased with them both, raised to the Prophet: ""'When the earth is shaken' equals half the Qur'an, 'Say: He is God, One' equals one third of the Qur'an, and 'Say: O disbelievers' equals one quarter of the Qur'an."" Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak and said: its chain is sound.

Since practical, volitional polytheism is more dominant over souls because of their following of their desires, and many of them commit it knowing its harm and falsehood, due to the worldly aims they gain from it, its removal and uprooting from them is harder and more difficult than uprooting and removing scholarly polytheism, because the latter disappears through knowledge and proof, and its adherent cannot know a thing other than as it is, unlike the polytheism of will and intention, for its adherent commits what knowledge shows to be false and harmful, due to the dominance of his desire and the domination of the authority of lust and anger over his self. Hence the emphasis and repetition in the surah "Say: O disbelievers", which includes the removal of practical polytheism, is equivalent to what comes in the surah "Say: He is God, One".

Since the Qur'an is two halves: one half concerning this world, its rulings, what relates to them, and events occurring in it, including the actions of the responsible and others, and one half concerning the Hereafter and what takes place in it; and since Surat "When the earth is shaken" is purified from beginning to end for this second half, mentioning only the Hereafter and what occurs regarding the conditions of the earth and its inhabitants, it equals half the Qur'an. Hence this hadith is most fitting to be sound. And God knows best.

(p-6303) Fifth: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Most scholars hold that Surat "Say: He is God, One" is Meccan, and it has been mentioned in the occasions of its revelation that the polytheists in Mecca asked about it, and that disbelievers among the People of the Book, the Jews, asked in Medina. There is no contradiction, for God revealed it in Mecca first, then when asked something similar He revealed it again. This is among what a group of scholars have mentioned, and they said: a verse or surah may be revealed twice or more. What is mentioned among the various occasions of revelation may all be true, and what is meant by this is that when a cause suitable to it arose, Gabriel descended and recited it to him to inform him that it contains the answer to that cause, even though the Messenger already knew it beforehand. End of quote.

The investigation into the meaning of revelation, in a way that removes such apparent contradictions, has already been detailed in the introduction to this tafsir and in other places within it, so refer back to it.

For this noble surah there are separate tafsirs, and among the best are two books by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah: one on its tafsir, and the second on the secret of its equalling one third of the Qur'an, so keep both. And God is the Guide.

(p-6294) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
Surah al-Ikhlas (Sincerity).
It is Meccan, and its verses number four.

Al-Bukhari narrated from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ sent a man in command of a detachment (sariyyah). He used to lead his companions in prayer and would finish his recitation with ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾. When they returned, they mentioned this to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said: "Ask him why he does that." They asked him, and he said: "Because it is the attribute of the Most Gracious, and I love to recite it." The Prophet ﷺ said: "Tell him that Allah, the Exalted, loves him."

Imam Ahmad narrated from Abu Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Say: He is Allah, the One is equal to a third of the Qur'an." It was also narrated by al-Bukhari in a different context.

Imam Ahmad narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b that "the polytheists said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'O Muhammad, tell us the lineage of your Lord.' So Allah, the Exalted, revealed this surah."

(p-6295) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, words:

[1–4] ﴿Say: He is Allah, the One﴾ ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] ﴿He begets not, nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] ﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4]

﴿Say: He﴾ means: the true report, confirmed by proof, about which there is no doubt. This is what the grammarians call the "story" (qissah), or the "matter" (hadith), or the "affair" (sha'n). Abu al-Su'ud said: The reason for placing it in this position, although no antecedent has been mentioned, is to indicate that it is so well known and prominent that everyone recalls it, every pointer points to it, and every pronoun refers back to it. ﴿Allah is One﴾, that is, one in divinity (uluhiyyah) and lordship (rububiyyah).

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ahad" (One) means "wahid" (one). Ibn al-Athir said: "al-Ahad" among His names, exalted is He, is the Unique who has always been alone, with no other with Him. Its hamza is a substitute for a waw, and its original form is "wahad," because it derives from wahdah (oneness).

In al-Misbah it is said: "ahad" is synonymous with "wahid" in two positions, by transmitted usage. The first: describing the Name of the Creator, exalted is He. One says: He is al-Wahid and He is al-Ahad, because He is exclusively characterized by oneness (ahadiyyah), so no other shares it with Him. For this reason, no one other than Allah, exalted is He, is described by it; one does not say "a man ahad" or "a dirham ahad" or the like.

The second position: the numerals, by prevalence and frequent usage; one says "ahad wa-'ishrun" and "wahid wa-'ishrun." In other contexts the difference between them in usage is that "ahad" is used to negate what is mentioned with it, so it is used only in negation, because it contains generality, as in: "No one (ahad) stood." Or when it is annexed, as in: "None (ahad) of the three stood." "Wahid" is the name for the first of a series of numbers, and it is used in affirmation, both annexed and unannexed; one says: "A certain (wahid) man of the people came to me." End of quotation.

(p-6296) Al-Azhari said: "Wahid" is among the attributes of Allah, exalted is He; its meaning is that He has no second. It is permissible to describe a thing as "wahid." But "ahad" is not used to describe anything other than Allah, exalted is He, because this noble name belongs exclusively to Him, may His praise be exalted.

The Imam (al-Razi) said: The predicate is indefinite (nukkira) because the intention is to inform about Allah that He is one, not that there is no one else besides Him. Oneness belongs to each individual; you say: "There is no one (ahad) in the house," meaning that no one among the people is in it. What the addressees were claiming was plurality within His essence, so He wished to negate that by saying He is "one." This is an affirmation contrary to what the two principles (usul) believers hold, such as the Magians, and what those who hold to the Trinity believe, both among themselves and others. Ibn Taymiyyah will later present another discussion on the secret of choosing indefiniteness.

﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] means: He to whom one turns in needs and to whom one directs desires, because the ultimate of lordship ends with Him. Al-Ghazali said this in al-Maqsad al-Asna. Likewise Ibn Jarir said: "al-Samad" among the Arabs is the lord (sayyid) to whom one turns, who has no one above him, and likewise their nobles are called by it. From this is the poet's verse:

"Has not the mourner come at dawn with news of the two best of Bani Asad,
of 'Amr ibn Mas'ud and of the eminent lord al-Samad?"

Al-Shihab said: It is "fa'al" in the sense of "maf'ul," and "samada" means "qasada" (to intend), so it is transitive by itself, and with the lam and with ila.

Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Regarding al-Samad, the early generations (al-salaf) held several opinions, which may seem to be different, but they are not; rather all of them are correct. The most well known of them are two:

The first: that al-Samad is the one who has no hollow (jawf).
The second: that He is the lord to whom one turns in needs.

The first is the view of most of the early generations among the Companions and the Successors, and of a group of the linguists. The second is the view of a group of the early and later scholars and of the majority of the lexicographers.

(p-6297) Then he, may Allah have mercy on him, expanded on the source of this term, its derivation, and what is transmitted about it, until he said:

The lam was added to "al-Samad" but not to "ahad," because among existing things there is nothing called "ahad" in affirmation, singular and unannexed; no entity is described by it except Allah alone. It is used for other than Allah only in negation, in annexation, and in the unrestricted numeral. As for the name "al-Samad," the linguists used it of created beings, as mentioned earlier. So He did not say "samad" but said ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2], clarifying that He alone is entitled to be the Samad, not what is other than Him, for He is the one who deserves His ultimate perfection. A created being, though it may be samad in some respects, does not truly possess the reality of samadiyyah, because it accepts division and fragmentation, and it is also in need of other than itself, for everything other than Allah is in need of Him in every respect. No one is someone to whom everything turns while he turns to nothing except Allah. In created things there is only what can be divided, separated, split, and detached, part from part. But Allah, glory be to Him, is the Samad to whom none of that can apply; rather the reality and perfection of samadiyyah belong to Him alone, necessarily and inseparably. It is impossible for His samadiyyah to be absent in any way, just as it is impossible for His oneness to be doubled in any way. End of quotation.

Abu al-Su'ud said: The repetition of the Glorious Name is to indicate that whoever does not possess these attributes is far from deserving divinity. The sentence is left without a conjunction because it is like a conclusion (natijah) of the first. First He stated His divinity (uluhiyyah), which entails all the attributes of perfection; then His oneness (ahadiyyah), which requires His transcendence above any trace of plurality and composition in any respect, and above any supposition of sharing in the essence and its properties; then His samadiyyah, which requires His essential self-sufficiency (istighna') from all other than Him and the need of all creatures for Him in their existence, their continuance, and all their conditions. This is to establish the truth and to guide them to His clear path. Then He explicitly mentioned some of what falls under what was previously stated, with His words, glory be to Him: ﴿He begets not﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3], refuting the claims of the slanderers concerning the angels and the Messiah. For this reason the negation came in the past tense form, meaning: no child has issued from Him, because nothing is of His kind, so that He could have a consort of His kind and they would beget. As His words, exalted is He, affirm: ﴿How can He have a child when He has no consort?﴾ And He has no need of anything that would help Him or succeed Him, because need and perishing are impossible for Him, glory be to Him. End of quotation.

(p-6298) Ibn Taymiyyah said: What He, glory be to Him, informed about includes His transcendence and sanctification above what they attributed to Him of begetting, in all its forms, whether they called it physical or intellectual. Like the Sabian philosophers claim about the generation of the ten intellects and the nine celestial souls, concerning which they are in dispute: are they substances or accidents? They sometimes make the intellects equivalent to males and the souls equivalent to females, and they make these their fathers, their mothers, their gods, and their nearest lords. This resembles the saying of the polytheists of the Arabs and others, who attributed to Him sons and daughters. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And they made the jinn partners with Allah, though He created them, and they falsely attributed to Him sons and daughters without knowledge. Glorified is He and high above what they describe﴾ [al-An'am: 100]. He also said: ﴿Surely they say out of their own lies﴾ [al-Saffat: 151] ﴿"Allah has begotten," and they are indeed liars﴾ [al-Saffat: 152]. They used to say: "The angels are the daughters of Allah." Likewise these people claim that the souls are the angels, and that they are generated from Allah. So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And they attribute daughters to Allah—glory be to Him—while for themselves is what they desire﴾ [al-Nahl: 57]. The verses on this are many.

His words ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 3] are a negation of any relation (nasab) encompassing Him from every direction. He is the First, to whom no parent preceded, and the Last, after whom no child will come to be from Him. The Imam (al-Razi) said: His words ﴿nor is He begotten﴾ clearly refute what some followers of religions claim: that a son of Allah could be a god, worshipped with the worship due to God, and that the Divine is intended in him. Rather, the extremists among them are not ashamed to call his mother "the Mother of the Powerful God." For the begotten is created and comes into being only through a temperament (mizaj), and he is not safe from the consequence of extinction. The claim that he is eternal together with his father is something that cannot be conceived. He, glory be to Him, is far above that.

﴿And there is none comparable to Him﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 4] means: no one equal to Him exists who could match Him, whether a consort or otherwise. The Imam said: "Kufu'" means one who is equal to and similar to Him in action and power. This is a negation of what some idolaters believe about, for example, Satan. In this surah He has negated all kinds of association (shirk) and established all the foundations of tawhid and tanzih. Ibn Jarir said: "al-kufu'," "al-kafi'," and "al-kifa'" are one and the same in the speech of the Arabs; they mean equal and like.

It is also read "kufuwan" with a damma on the kaf and the fa', and the hamza changed into a waw. It is also read with the fa' sukun and with the hamza; these are two well-known readings and two famous dialects. The word "lahu" is a complement to "kufuwan," placed before it although its natural place is after it, for emphasis, because the intention is to negate equal recompense from His essence, exalted is He. As for the delay of the subject of "kana," it is for the sake of preserving the rhyme (fawasil).

Benefits from this surah:

The first: Al-Shihab said: If you ask: the one addressed by "Say" (qul), when he complies, should only utter what is said. Why is "Say" among what is recited in it and in similar passages? I answer: The one commanded, whether specified or not, is commanded to affirm what is said, so He affirmed the saying in order to indicate the obligation of what is said and the necessity of affirming it throughout the ages.

The second: Imam Ibn Taymiyyah said: Some proponents of innovated speculative theology (kalam) have argued from His words ﴿Allah, the Eternal Refuge﴾ [al-Ikhlas: 2] that the Lord, exalted is He, is a body (jism). Like some who agreed with Hisham ibn al-Hakam, Muhammad ibn Karram, and others, they said: He is samad, and the samad is that which has no hollow. This applies only to solid bodies, which have no hollow, such as mountains, rocks, and what is made of columns of stone. For this reason it was said in its explanation that He is that from which nothing comes out and into which nothing enters, and who neither eats nor drinks. The negation of this is conceivable only of what is a body.

They also said: The root of "samad" is gathering, and from it comes "tasmid al-mal" (piling up of wealth). This is conceivable only of a gathered body. But the negators said: "al-Samad" is the one to whom division and separation cannot apply, and every body in the world is subject to division and separation. They also said: "al-Ahad" is the one who does not accept partition or division, and every body in the world is subject to separation, partition, and division. They said: If you say He is a body, He would be composed (murakkab) and assembled (mu'allaf) (p-6300) of single particles (jawahir fardah) or of matter and form. Whatever is composed and assembled of other things is in need of them, and He, glory be to Him, is the samad, and the samad is the one free of need of others. So the composite cannot be samad. End of quotation.

Since the Qur'an is two halves: one half concerning this world, its rulings, what relates to them, and events occurring in it, including the actions of the responsible and others, and one half concerning the Hereafter and what takes place in it; and since Surat "When the earth is shaken" is purified from beginning to end for this second half, mentioning only the Hereafter and what occurs regarding the conditions of the earth and its inhabitants, it equals half the Qur'an. Hence this hadith is most fitting to be sound. And God knows best.

(p-6303) Fifth: Ibn Taymiyyah said: Most scholars hold that Surat "Say: He is God, One" is Meccan, and it has been mentioned in the occasions of its revelation that the polytheists in Mecca asked about it, and that disbelievers among the People of the Book, the Jews, asked in Medina. There is no contradiction, for God revealed it in Mecca first, then when asked something similar He revealed it again. This is among what a group of scholars have mentioned, and they said: a verse or surah may be revealed twice or more. What is mentioned among the various occasions of revelation may all be true, and what is meant by this is that when a cause suitable to it arose, Gabriel descended and recited it to him to inform him that it contains the answer to that cause, even though the Messenger already knew it beforehand. End of quote.

The investigation into the meaning of revelation, in a way that removes such apparent contradictions, has already been detailed in the introduction to this tafsir and in other places within it, so refer back to it.

For this noble surah there are separate tafsirs, and among the best are two books by Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah: one on its tafsir, and the second on the secret of its equalling one third of the Qur'an, so keep both. And God is the Guide.
